title: Modals
subtitle: Ability, permission, advice, criticism, obligation and necessity, degrees of certainty

items: All modals (**will, would, shall, should, can, could, may, might, must**) and the semi-modal **ought to** have only one form.
Modals are followed by the bare infinitive (simple or continuous) or the bare perfect infinitive: Toby **should be** very fit by now. · Toby **should have recovered** by now.
The semi-modals **have to** and **need** to change their form depending on person and tense: The doctor said I **had/needed to** give up red meat.

rows.use: Expressing ability now or generally · can
rows.example: I **can** run a kilometre in four minutes.

rows.use: Expressing decisions made now about future ability · can
rows.example: We **can** meet at the gym tomorrow, if you like.

rows.use: Expressing ability in the past · could
rows.example: I **could** do fifty press-ups with one hand when I was younger.

rows.use: Expressing ability in present, future or general hypothetical situations · could
Expressing ability in past hypothetical situations · could + perfect infinitive
rows.example: I **could have roasted** the potatoes, but I decided that boiling them was healthier.

blocks.text: We use **be able to** for the infinitive and other tenses.
blocks.note: I'd love **to be able to** fit into these jeans again! (infinitive) · I'll **be able to** leave hospital in a few weeks, apparently. (future) · I've **been able to** swim since I was five. (present perfect)

rows.use: Asking for and giving permission now, for the future or generally · may / could / can
rows.example: **May / Could / Can** I see the doctor, please?

blocks.text: **May** is more polite than **could**, and **could** is more polite than **can**.

blocks.correct: I **was allowed to** wear a knee support during the match.
blocks.incorrect: I **could wear** a knee support during the match.

blocks.text: We don't usually use **could** to talk about past permission. However, we do use **could** to talk about past permission in reported speech.
blocks.note: The coach said I **could** wear a knee support during the match.

rows.use: Asking for and giving advice now, for the future or generally · should / ought to
rows.example: You **ought to / should** cut down on the amount of red meat you eat.

rows.use: Criticising past behaviour · should / ought to + perfect infinitive
rows.example: He **ought to / should have made** more of an effort with his diet.

rows.use: Expressing obligation or necessity · must / have to / need to
rows.example: I **must / have to / need to** pick up that prescription from the chemist on the way home.

rows.use: Expressing lack of obligation or necessity · needn't / don't have to / don't need to
rows.example: You **needn't / don't have to / don't need to** pick up that prescription from the chemist as I'll get it while I'm in town.
I **had to** take the pills three times a day for two weeks.

rows.use: Expressing lack of past obligation · needn't + perfect infinitive / didn't have to / didn't need to
rows.example: I **needn't have gone** / **didn't have to go** / **didn't need to go** to the doctor.

items: There is usually no difference in meaning between **must** and **have to**. However, we are sometimes more likely to use **must** for personal obligation and **have to** for external obligation.
We can also use **will have/need to** to express future obligation: You'll **have/need to** be more careful about what you eat in future.
It is unusual to use **must** for questions. We usually use **have/need to**: **Do I have/need to** take this medicine before every meal?
**Must** cannot be used as an infinitive. Use **to have to**: I'd hate **to have to** have injections every day.

**Mustn't** and **don't/doesn't have/need to** have different meanings. **You mustn't do that!** (Don't do that!) · **You don't have/need to do that.** (You can do it if you want to but it's not necessary.)

**Needn't** + perfect infinitive always refers to actions that happened. **Didn't have to** and **didn't need to** can refer to actions that did or didn't happen: I **needn't have gone** to the doctor. (I went but it wasn't necessary.) · I **didn't have/need to** go to the doctor because I suddenly felt better. (I didn't go.) · I **didn't have/need to** go to the doctor but I went just to be on the safe side. (I did go.)
Be careful with the verb **need**. It can also take the **-ing** form: I **need to sterilise** this syringe. · This syringe **needs sterilising**.

rows.use: Expressing certainty (or near certainty) about now or generally · must / can't / couldn't
rows.example: That **must** be the district nurse at the door. · These **can't / couldn't** be the pills; they're the wrong colour.

rows.use: Expressing certainty (or near certainty) about the past · must / can't / couldn't + perfect infinitive
rows.example: She **must have been** in a lot of pain. · His leg **can't / couldn't have been** in plaster for two years!

rows.use: Expressing probability about now, the future or generally · should / ought to
rows.example: You **ought to / should** feel better in a few days, as long as you get lots of rest.

rows.use: Expressing probability about the past · should / ought to + perfect infinitive
rows.example: The bruise **ought to / should have disappeared** days ago. I wonder why it didn't.

rows.use: Expressing possibility about now, the future or generally · could / may / might
rows.example: You **should** ask your doctor first because that diet **could / may / might** be dangerous.

rows.use: Expressing possibility about the real past · could / may / might + perfect infinitive
rows.example: That **could / may / might have been** the doctor who rang earlier while we were out.

rows.use: Expressing possibility about a hypothetical past · could / might + perfect infinitive
rows.example: It's a good thing you went to the doctor or you **could / might have become** quite ill.

exercises.title: A · Tick or correct
exercises.instruction: If a word or phrase in bold is correct, write it again. If it is incorrect, rewrite it correctly.

items.prompt: Can you **to speak** French?
I **can** give you a hand tomorrow morning, if you like.
I'll **can** take my driving test after a few more lessons.
Jack **can** play the guitar before he learnt to talk!
If only I **can** afford to buy that top!
We **can have gone** up the Eiffel Tower while we were in Paris, but we decided to go to the Louvre instead.
I **could get** a more expensive computer, but it didn't seem worth it.
I wish I **could** get out of the maths test tomorrow!
I bet you'd love to **be can to** get satellite TV.
You'd better tell the coach if you can't **playing** on Saturday.

exercises.instruction: Select the form that fits. If both forms are possible, choose the option that says both.

exercises.title: C · must, have to, need
exercises.instruction: Write a form of must, have to, need or need to in each gap. If more than one possibility is correct, write the most natural one; other accepted forms also score.

items.prompt: Oh, I ___ remember to get some potatoes on the way home tonight.

We ___ light lots of candles during the power cut two nights ago.

We ___ do any washing-up after the picnic because we'd used disposable plates and cutlery.

I ___ have bothered cooking all that food; they'd eaten before they arrived.

exercises.title: D · Similar meaning
exercises.instruction: Complete each second sentence using the word given, so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Write between two and five words.

items.prompt:
His lights are on so I'm pretty sure Dan is at home. **as**
Dan ___ his lights are on.

Susie's car's not here so she's almost certainly taking Dobber to the vet. **be**
Susie ___ Dobber to the vet since her car's not here.

There's no way that boy's Simon. He's much taller! **boy**
That ___ Simon. He's much taller!

I'm certain the Winners don't think we're coming tonight; we arranged it for next Tuesday. **expecting**
The Winners ___ tonight; we arranged it for next Tuesday.

I bet you were exhausted after such a long journey! **have**
You ___ exhausted after such a long journey!

The only explanation is that Evan was on the phone to someone in Australia! **talking**
Evan ___ on the phone to someone in Australia!

There's no way Casey won the disco dancing competition — he's got two left feet! **have**
Casey ___ the disco dancing competition — he's got two left feet!

I don't believe Helen's been trying to call us all day. The phone hasn't rung once. **been**
Helen ___ to call us all day. The phone hasn't rung once.

exercises.title: E · Modals in Table A
exercises.instruction: Use the words in the box only once to complete the sentences. The meaning in Table B will help you.

items.prompt: I ___ have left my bag on the bus. (expressing certainty)
In a few months, I'll be ___ to buy a car. (expressing future ability)
I ___ drive when I was thirteen years old! (expressing past ability)
No, you ___ have any more pocket money! (refusing a request)
I think you ___ consider a career in the armed forces. (giving advice)
I ___ forget to phone Julie tonight! (expressing personal obligation)
I ___ to have a filling at the dentist's. (expressing external obligation in the past)
You don't ___ to do Exercise D for homework. (expressing a lack of obligation)
You ___ have to work a lot harder if you want to get a good report. (expressing future obligation)
They ___ to arrive at about 8. (expressing probability)
Sean ___ have got stuck in traffic. (expressing possibility)
I ___ have worried so much about Jan's present. She loved it! (expressing a lack of past obligation)

exercises.title: G · Replace the phrase
exercises.instruction: Write a modal or semi-modal in each gap to replace the phrase in brackets. Add any other words you need.

items.prompt: Bruce ___ finish most crosswords in under ten minutes. (is able to)
Charlotte didn't get to the Craig David concert because she ___ get tickets. (wasn't able to)
I ___ go to Oxford but I decided to go to a more modern university. (had the opportunity to go)
You ___ Angus. You know he can't keep a secret! (were wrong to tell)
If you have a cashpoint card, you ___ go into the bank to get money from your account. (are not forced to)
We ___ apologise to the police for wasting their time. (were made to)
That ___ the last can of soda in the fridge. I bought loads this morning! (almost definitely wasn't)
___ talk about two photographs during the interview? (Were you obliged to)
Children ___ be left unattended. (are not allowed to)
The weather ___ be good tomorrow. (will probably)

exercises.title: H · Choosing a gym
exercises.instruction: Select the form that completes each gap.

items.prompt: Choosing to go to a gym regularly ___ change your life for the better. Don't let it be a decision you regret!
Good gyms have a lot to offer. They ___ provide exercise equipment that is just too expensive to buy
and their trained staff are ___ to provide quality health and fitness advice.
But if you're planning to join a gym, you ___ definitely ask to look round before you become a member.
There are a number of things to bear in mind before choosing which gym to join. Before the law changed a few years ago, anyone ___ set up a gym and even today gyms
___ employ trained fitness instructors. Find out what qualifications the staff have.
If they're untrained, it's best to go elsewhere. You ___ be put off by the gym's hard sell.
Just because they want you to sign up — they want your money, after all — that doesn't mean you ___ decide there and then.

See a few gyms before you make your final decision. Ask yourself: What kind of equipment and facilities do they have? There's little point joining a gym and then thinking a few months later, 'I ___ have chosen a gym with a pool.'
Do you ___ book equipment in advance, or can you just turn up and use it?
How busy does the gym get? It ___ be very pleasant turning up to find there's no room in the changing room and there's a huge queue for each piece of equipment.
It ___ also be a good idea to talk to people who already go to that gym to find out their opinion.

exercises.title: I · One word in each gap
exercises.instruction: Write one word in each gap.

items.prompt: When I broke my arm a week ago, I guess it (1) ___ to have hurt. But it didn't!
We were doing PE at school, and we were making a pyramid. We (2) ___ to stand on each other's shoulders.
I was right at the top. We (3) ___ have been doing it properly because suddenly the pyramid collapsed and we all fell.
I landed on my arm. Mr Jenkins (4) ___ have known immediately that I'd broken my arm because he sent someone to call an ambulance.
'Sit still, and don't move your arm at all until the ambulance comes,' he said. I (5) ___ still remember the feeling — my arm was numb, and looked very strange, but there was no pain at all.
I remember thinking: 'It (6) ___ be broken. If it was broken, I'd be in agony.'
I suppose not feeling any pain (7) ___ have been because I was in shock.
The plaster ___ come off in about three weeks but I may have to stay on longer.
The plaster should come off in about three weeks but I ___ have to stay on longer.
The next three weeks may ___ be the best three weeks of my life — no basketball, no playing in the playground, no swimming — but I'm counting my blessings.
It ___ have been a lot worse!
